title: Learn Technical Writing
tagline: From confusing READMEs to docs people can actually follow
description: A three-level curriculum for Technical Writers. Learn plain language and docs-as-code, then document APIs and product workflows with engineers, then run a docs system — style, versioning, and measurement — so users and teammates can finish the job without a Slack thread.
prerequisites: Strong writing in the language you will document in (usually English)
Comfort reading technical material even if you do not write production code
Willingness to ask 'dumb' questions until the steps are actually true

levels.title: Writing & Docs Foundations
levels.goal: Write task-oriented docs in Markdown, with structure a reader can scan

topics.title: Plain language
items: Active voice, short sentences, and one idea per paragraph
Procedures vs. concepts vs. reference — do not mix them in one page
Cutting jargon, or defining it the first time

topics.title: Audience & jobs
items: Who is this page for, and what are they trying to finish?
Beginner vs. expert readers; onboarding vs. lookup
Error messages, UI copy, and docs as one voice

topics.title: Findability
items: Table of contents, headings, and page titles that match search
Task-oriented IA: getting started, how-to, reference, troubleshooting
When a page should split; when it should stay one screen

topics.title: Structure of a how-to
items: Prerequisites, numbered steps, expected result, next step
Screenshots and when they rot
Warnings, notes, and troubleshooting that is not a dump

topics.title: Markdown & Git
items: Headings, lists, links, code fences, and tables
Branches, PRs, and review comments on docs
Previewing locally so you do not ship broken links

topics.title: Working in a docs repo
items: File naming, folders, and front matter
Linking between pages without circular mazes
Style sheet: do/don't for the team

projects: Rewrite a confusing README into a task-oriented getting-started
How-to with numbered steps, prerequisites, and an expected result
IA map for a small product: getting started, how-tos, reference, troubleshooting
One-page style sheet (voice, terms, formatting) a teammate could follow

levels.title: Documenting Products & APIs
levels.goal: Document APIs and user workflows accurately by working with subject-matter experts

topics.title: OpenAPI & reference
items: Reading an OpenAPI spec: paths, params, and error codes
Descriptions that say what and when, not only the type
Auth, pagination, idempotency, and rate limits in human language

topics.title: Code samples
items: Minimal working examples (curl, then one language)
Request/response that match the live API
Common errors and how to recover

topics.title: Getting started
items: Time-to-first-success: one happy path before every option
Accounts, keys, and sandbox vs. production
Checklists vs. narrative — pick for the job

topics.title: Product how-tos
items: Documenting a UI flow without screenshot rot
Permissions, roles, and 'you cannot see this because'
Release notes that a human can scan

topics.title: SME interviews
items: Prep: read the ticket, the PR, and the last doc
Questions that extract steps, not architecture lectures
Confirming facts: you write, they correct, you own the page

topics.title: Accuracy & review
items: Trying the steps yourself (Postman, CLI, or UI)
Review checklists: correctness, completeness, and tone
Tracking doc bugs the same way as product bugs

projects: Getting-started guide for a sample API (auth, one write, one read, one error)
OpenAPI descriptions and examples for five endpoints
User guide for a feature with roles, empty states, and a troubleshooting section
Interview an engineer (or a recorded talk), then write a page they will sign off as accurate

levels.title: Docs Systems at Scale
levels.goal: Run documentation as a product: style, versioning, contribution, and whether people succeed

topics.title: Style guides that stick
items: Terminology, product names, and inclusive language
Linting (Vale) and PR templates for docs
Who can merge; who must review for accuracy

topics.title: Contribution models
items: Engineers as authors vs. writers as editors
Templates for how-tos, concepts, and API pages
Internal runbooks vs. customer docs — same craft, different audience

topics.title: Docs that match the product
items: Versioning docs with API or app releases
Deprecations, breaking changes, and migration guides
Feature flags and 'this page is for the new flow'

topics.title: Release communication
items: Changelogs vs. release notes vs. migration guides
Support macros and docs staying in sync
Localization awareness: what does not translate

topics.title: Effectiveness
items: Search queries, bounce, and time-to-first-success
Support tickets that should have been a page
Feedback widgets without drowning in noise

topics.title: Docs as a product
items: Backlog, prioritization, and saying no to a wiki dump
On-call for docs: broken steps after a release
Ethics: security-sensitive procedures and what not to publish

projects: Docs site (Docusaurus or MkDocs) with IA, getting started, and API reference
Style guide plus contribution model and a PR template
Migration guide for a breaking API or UI change, versioned next to the old docs
Docs quality report: search/support evidence and three improvements you would ship first
